We are a team of 10th grade students from TED İzmir College in Türkiye, participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our team brings together different perspectives and ideas with a shared goal of learning, collaborating, and creating something meaningful.

Throughout this challenge, we aim to make the most of our individual strengths, learn from one another, and approach challenges with an open mind.

We look forward to gaining new experiences and developing our skills.

details:
The Voice of the Two Orbits

Guests of the Moon

Our Project

We created an engaging, historically accurate audio drama about NASA’s 1969 Apollo 12 mission and its historic meeting with the unmanned Surveyor 3 spacecraft on the Moon. Usually, videos and articles about space are full of heavy technical details, making it hard for people, especially children, to feel emotionally connected to the story. Our project solves this problem by combining real NASA radio recordings and the true personalities of astronauts Pete Conrad, Alan Bean, and Richard F. Gordon Jr. with a creative twist: giving a voice to Surveyor 3, which waited alone on the Moon for two and a half years. Using sound effects, expressive storytelling, and emotional voice acting, we turn cold historical facts into a warm, memorable story. This project matters because it makes space history fun and easy to understand, sparking kids' curiosity about science and engineering.

Project Description & Functionality

The Guests of the Moon audio drama functions as an immersive educational podcast tailored for children. Our project combines storytelling, voice acting, digital media, and open science education to make historical space data accessible and enjoyable for younger generations. With our podcast, we aim to transform how children perceive space science—shifting it from "boring data" to an exciting adventure.

How It Works & Open Data Utilization

Our project is directly powered by NASA’s open-access historical archives, telemetry records, and authentic mission transcripts. We leveraged these open-source space databases to extract real-world events—such as the Apollo 12 lightning strike logs and Surveyor 3's lunar surface data—and translated them into an emotionally engaging narrative. By combining authentic radio logs with expressive voice acting, we bridged the gap between raw scientific data and public accessibility.

Tools, Technologies & Development

To bring this project to life, our team utilized the following tools and resources:

Audio & Production: Original voice acting performed by our team members (Asya Çardak, Doğa Özen, İlke Savran, and Kayra Aras). We edited the audio and added sound effects and atmospheric music using CapCut, sourcing our audio effects and background tracks from YouTube, Freesound.org, and Pixabay.com.

Open Data & Research: Official NASA mission transcripts and public historical archives.

Web Design & Presentation: Canva and web design tools to create an attractive, user-friendly, and engaging platform where visitors can explore our project and podcast script.

Target Audience & Creative Considerations

While developing the project, we carefully considered our target audience, particularly children's interests, attention spans, and varying levels of scientific knowledge. We ensured our content was both educational and entertaining without making scientific topics overwhelming.

The Story & Characters

The story of our audio drama follows astronauts Pete Conrad, Alan Bean, and Richard F. Gordon Jr. Another main character is Surveyor 3, portrayed as the grumpy, lonely resident of the Moon. While our characters are slightly stylized to better appeal to children, they are all rooted in real history. To maintain absolute authenticity, we integrated genuine historical quotes from the astronauts into our script, paired with the creative twist of giving a voice to Surveyor 3, which waited in silence on the lunar surface since 1967.
